overview.title: 📖 Overview: When Does Nullification Truly Erase Impurity?
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 23a–23b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf pursues the question raised at the end of 22b: can impurity that was nullified within a majority ever be reawakened? Ulla's decree about teruma mixed into non-sacred produce, and a running set of objections from Abaye involving red heifer ashes and carcass meat, test whether nullification is a permanent erasure or only a suppression that a new 'match' can revive — a question that circles back directly to the mass of congealed blood from the previous daf. A related dispute between bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan asks how long a decaying carcass keeps transmitting impurity at all. The Gemara then applies these same principles to brine purchased from an unreliable seller, before the daf's new mishna turns to a very different concern: purchasing a nursing animal from a gentile, and whether one must worry its milk actually belongs to another mother's offspring.

slides.title: ♻️ Can Nullified Impurity Ever Revive?
slides.subtitle: Ulla's decree launches a chain of challenges from Abaye

lines.speaker: Ulla
lines.text: Even a nullified teruma-in-chullin mixture may not touch water — a decree lest someone deliberately add more impure produce, thinking the majority will nullify it too, when in fact the small existing trace 'finds its own kind' and revives.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: That proves impurity can revive impurity. But does pure water revive impurity, as claimed for the fish brine?

lines.speaker: Abaye's Challenge
lines.text: From red heifer ashes mixed with ordinary ashes: if nullified impurity still 'exists' in some sense, the mixture should at least impart impurity through carrying, even if not by touch!

lines.speaker: Rav Dimi
lines.text: Indeed — Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Ḥanina rules exactly that: pure from impurity by contact, but impure via carrying.

lines.speaker: Abaye's Challenge
lines.text: Then apply the same logic to carcass meat nullified within slaughtered meat — it too should impart impurity via carrying!

lines.speaker: Final Challenge
lines.text: But our own mishna states the mass of congealed blood does not impart impurity even via carrying! Rav Dimi had no answer — and fell silent.

callout.label: Left open:
callout.text: The question of whether nullification is total or reversible remains unresolved at this point in the sugya.

slides.title: 🐕 How Long Does a Carcass Keep Imparting Impurity?
slides.subtitle: Bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute when decay ends impurity

boxes.title: Bar Padda — Two Standards
items: Severe impurity (e.g. a stillbirth) lasts until the item is no longer fit even for a ger toshav (resident alien permitted such food)
Light impurity (an ordinary carcass) lasts only until unfit for a dog
Derived from Deuteronomy 14:21: 'you may give it to the ger' — only what's fit for a ger is called 'a carcass' at all

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan — One Standard
items: Both severe and light impurity last only until the item is no longer fit for a dog
The verse instead excludes only meat that decayed from the very start, before ever becoming edible

boxes.title: The Difficulty
items: On Rabbi Yoḥanan's view, since the congealed mass IS still fit for a dog, it should still impart impurity
Yet the mishna rules it does not — the Gemara leaves this 'קַשְׁיָא', a genuine difficulty

callout.label: Shared source:
callout.text: Both opinions read the same verse — 'you shall not eat of any carcass... you may give it to the ger' — but draw different lines from it.

slides.title: 🩸 Why 'Nullified,' Not 'Never Fit'?
slides.subtitle: Returning to the mass of congealed blood with a sharper question

nodes.content: ❓ Rabbi Yoḥanan attributes the mass's purity to nullification in a majority. Why not simply say it was never fit for consumption at all?
🔎 Because it WAS fit for consumption at one point — through its mother
✅ Had the mother been slaughtered before the mass emerged, it would have been edible as ordinary meat, as part of her body
🎓 So its later loss of edibility requires the active mechanism of nullification, not a claim that it was 'always' unfit

callout.label: Why this matters:
callout.text: The distinction determines whether the mass could ever regain significance — an item 'never fit' has no such potential, but a nullified item might, as the earlier debate over reviving impurity shows.

slides.title: 🧂 Brine and the Suspected Peddlers
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: pure brine bought from a gentile, with any water added, becomes impure
rows: Pure brine into which any amount of water falls becomes impure
This shows amei ha'aretz (unreliable sellers) are suspected of secretly mixing roughly half water into the brine they sell
Why assume specifically 'half'? Even less water mixed in should also revive the impurity!
Say instead they're suspected of mixing in water up to just under half
Both layers of impurity here (an am ha'aretz's food, and liquids) are only rabbinic; the Sages decreed impurity only for a true majority of water, not for an even half-half split

callout.label: Practical upshot:
callout.text: A tiny addition of water is enough to revive suspected impurity, precisely because the seller is assumed to have already diluted the brine close to the tipping point.

slides.title: 🐑 A Nursing Animal — and Rav Sheshet's Process of Elimination
slides.subtitle: New mishna, then a puzzle over what Rav's blanket ruling could possibly mean

steps.content: 1️⃣ New mishna: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules one who buys a nursing animal from a gentile — or sees mixed first-time and repeat mothers nursing in his own flock — need not worry the offspring were swapped
2️⃣ Rav (via Rav Naḥman): 'The halakha follows the anonymous first tanna throughout this whole chapter, except where a dispute is recorded'
3️⃣ Rav Sheshet objects: which mishna could this mean? Not the chapter's opening mishna — Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva openly disagree there
4️⃣ Not Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling either — his opinions are already known to be reliably authoritative ('a kav that is small but clean')
5️⃣ Not Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling as stated, since an outside baraita records a dissent — nor two later mishnayot, each already resolved or disputed on its own
6️⃣ Conclusion: it must be Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling after all — Rav teaches that a dissent recorded only in an outside baraita doesn't count as a real 'dispute' for this purpose

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: Rav Sheshet works through every candidate mishna in the chapter by elimination before the Gemara lands on the answer.

summary.principle: Nullification in a majority removes an item's independent halakhic force, but whether that suppression can be 'reawakened' by contact with its own kind — in impurity, in a carcass's decay, or in diluted brine — remains a live and only partially resolved question.

flowSteps.content: ♻️ Abaye's chain of challenges tests whether nullified impurity can ever revive — left unresolved for the congealed mass
🐕 Bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute how long a decaying carcass keeps transmitting impurity at all
🩸 The congealed mass needed nullification, not 'never fit,' since it was once edible via its mother

columns.content: 🧂 Even a trace of water can revive suspected impurity in brine from an unreliable seller
🐑 Rav Sheshet eliminates candidates to find which mishna Rav's blanket ruling really targets

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Nullification suppresses a minority presence, but the Gemara treats that suppression as fragile — reversible whenever the right conditions recur

quiz.q: According to Ulla, why did the Sages decree that a fully nullified mixture of teruma and non-sacred produce may not touch water?
o: Because water always creates new impurity from nothing
Lest someone deliberately add more impure produce, mistakenly believing the majority will nullify it too, when the existing trace could 'revive' the impurity
Because teruma may never touch any liquid under any circumstances
Because the mixture is always considered fully sacred
quiz.e: Ulla explains this as a rabbinic decree guarding against someone adding a similar impure substance and assuming it too gets nullified, when in fact the surviving trace of the original impurity can 'find its own kind' and become active again.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Ḥanina, what is the status of a mixture of red heifer ashes and ordinary ashes where the ordinary ashes are the majority?
o: Impure by both contact and carrying
Pure by contact, but still imparts impurity via carrying
Fully pure with no impurity whatsoever
The mixture must be buried immediately
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Ḥanina rules that although the mixture does not impart impurity through direct contact (since one is assumed to touch the majority), it still imparts impurity through carrying, since the minority of red heifer ash remains present.

quiz.q: According to bar Padda, based on Deuteronomy 14:21, what determines when an item with severe impurity (like a stillbirth) stops imparting impurity?
o: When it is no longer fit to be eaten by a dog
When it is no longer fit to be eaten by a ger toshav (resident alien permitted such food)
Impurity from such an item never ends
It stops immediately upon death
quiz.e: Bar Padda derives from the verse 'you may give it to the ger' that only an item fit for a ger toshav retains the halakhic label 'carcass' and its impurity; severe impurity therefore persists until the item is no longer fit even for a ger toshav.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara explain that the mass of congealed blood's purity comes specifically from 'nullification,' rather than simply saying it was 'never fit for consumption'?
o: Because it is currently being eaten by people
Because it had once been fit for consumption via its mother, had she been slaughtered before it emerged
Because the mishna never actually discusses its edibility
Because nullification and 'never fit' mean the exact same thing
quiz.e: The Gemara clarifies that the mass was initially fit for consumption as part of its mother's body (had she been slaughtered first), so its current lack of status requires the active mechanism of nullification rather than a claim that it was inherently unfit from the start.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling, what happens to pure brine purchased from a gentile if any amount of water falls into it?
o: Nothing changes — the brine remains pure
The brine becomes impure
The water becomes pure instead
The mixture must be immediately discarded without further discussion
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that even a small amount of water falling into otherwise pure brine renders it impure, which the Gemara explains reflects a suspicion that unreliable sellers (amei ha'aretz) had already diluted the brine close to the tipping point.
